question: What is HTML?
description: HTML (HyperText Markup Language) is the standard markup language for creating web pages. It structures content on the web using elements defined by tags, such as headings, paragraphs, and images. HTML provides the backbone of a webpage, which is styled with CSS and made interactive with JavaScript.
code:
Welcome to HTML

This is a paragraph.
note: This creates a simple webpage with a heading and paragraph.

question: What is the Structure of an HTML Document?
description: An HTML document follows a standard structure: a <!DOCTYPE html> declaration, followed by an <html> root element containing <head> (for metadata) and <body> (for visible content). The <head> includes elements like <title>, while <body> contains the page’s content.
note: This is a basic HTML document structure.

question: What is the Difference Between <div> and <span>?
description: <div> is a block-level element that creates a new line and takes up the full width of its container, used for grouping content. <span> is an inline element that doesn’t break the flow, used for styling small portions of text.
code:
This is a div.

This is a red word.
note: The div creates a block, while the span styles text inline.

question: How to Create a Hyperlink in HTML?
description: The <a> tag creates a hyperlink, using the href attribute to specify the destination URL. Additional attributes like target="_blank" open links in a new tab.
note: This creates a clickable link to an external website.

question: What is the Purpose of the <head> Tag?
description: The <head> tag contains metadata about the document, such as the page title (<title>), character encoding (<meta charset>), links to stylesheets (<link>), and scripts (<script>). It doesn’t display content on the page but provides information to browsers and search engines.
note: This sets up metadata for the webpage.

question: How to Add Images in HTML?
description: The tag adds images to a webpage, using the src attribute for the image URL and alt for accessibility. It’s a self-closing tag.
note: This displays an image with an alt description.

question: What is the Difference Between <ul> and <ol>?
description: <ul> (unordered list) creates a bulleted list, while <ol> (ordered list) creates a numbered list. Both use <li> tags for list items.
note: This creates a bulleted and a numbered list.

question: How to Create a Form in HTML?
description: The <form> tag creates a form for user input, using elements like <input>, <textarea>, and <button>. Attributes like action and method specify where and how data is sent.
code:
<form action="/submit" method="POST">
  <label for="name">Name:</label>
  <input type="text" id="name" name="name">
  <button type="submit">Submit</button>
</form>
note: This creates a simple form for submitting a name.

question: What is Semantic HTML?
description: Semantic HTML uses tags that convey meaning about the content, like <header>, <footer>, <article>, and <section>. It improves accessibility, SEO, and code readability compared to generic tags like <div>.
note: This uses semantic tags for better structure.

question: Why Does Semantic HTML5 Matter for SEO and Accessibility at Scale?
description: Semantic elements like <article>, <section>, <nav>, and <aside> describe the role of content, not just its appearance. Search engine crawlers use this structure to understand which content is primary versus supplementary, which directly affects how pages are indexed and ranked. Screen readers build a navigable outline from semantic landmarks, letting assistive-technology users jump straight to <nav>, <main>, or <aside> instead of tabbing through every element. A <div>-only page conveys none of this — visually identical, but structurally meaningless to both bots and assistive tech. In production codebases, overusing <div> also makes CSS selectors and component boundaries harder to reason about, so semantic tags pay off in maintainability too.
code:

Semantic tags give meaning to structure...

note: Each landmark (nav, main, aside, footer) is announced by screen readers and used by crawlers to build a content outline — a div can never do that.

question: How Do You Build an Accessible Form Using ARIA and Focus Management?
description: Accessible forms start with native semantics — a <label for="id"> tied to its input is worth more than any ARIA attribute, because it gives the field a name AND expands the click target. ARIA should only fill gaps native HTML can't cover: aria-describedby links an input to helper or error text so screen readers announce it alongside the label, aria-invalid="true" flags a field that failed validation, and an aria-live="polite" region announces async validation results without stealing focus. Focus management matters for dynamic forms: when an error appears, moving focus to the first invalid field (or announcing it via aria-live) prevents keyboard and screen-reader users from submitting into a void. The rule of thumb, per the WAI-ARIA spec, is 'no ARIA is better than bad ARIA' — use native elements first.
code:
We'll never share your email.

Please enter a valid email address.
note: On failed validation, set aria-invalid="true", unhide #email-error, and move focus to the input — role="alert" makes screen readers announce it immediately.

question: What Is the Critical Rendering Path, and How Do preload, prefetch, defer, and async Optimize It?
description: The critical rendering path is the sequence the browser follows to turn HTML/CSS/JS into pixels: parse HTML into the DOM, parse CSS into the CSSOM, combine them into a render tree, compute layout, then paint. CSS in <head> and synchronous <script> tags are render-blocking by default — the parser stops to fetch and execute them before continuing. <link rel="preload"> tells the browser to fetch a critical resource (a font, hero image, or key script) early and in parallel, without blocking rendering, so it's ready the instant it's needed. <link rel="prefetch"> is the opposite priority — it fetches a low-priority resource likely needed for a *future* navigation, using idle bandwidth. On <script>, defer downloads in parallel but delays execution until after HTML parsing completes (in document order), while async downloads in parallel and executes as soon as it's ready, potentially interrupting the parser — defer is almost always the safer default for scripts that touch the DOM.
code:
<head>
  <!-- Fetch the hero font early, in parallel with HTML parsing -->
  <link rel="preload" href="/fonts/inter.woff2" as="font" type="font/woff2" crossorigin>

  <!-- Warm the cache for a likely next page -->
  <link rel="prefetch" href="/checkout.html">

  <!-- Runs after parsing, in order -->
  <script src="/app.js" defer></script>

  <!-- Runs as soon as it loads, order not guaranteed -->
  <script src="/analytics.js" async></script>
</head>
note: Use preload for resources this page needs now, prefetch for resources the next page will need, defer for app scripts, and async for independent scripts like analytics.

question: What Are Web Components, and When Should You Reach for Them Instead of a Framework?
description: Web Components are a set of native browser APIs — Custom Elements (define your own <my-widget> tag with lifecycle callbacks), Shadow DOM (attach an encapsulated DOM subtree so the component's internal markup and CSS can't leak out or be overridden by page styles), and HTML Templates (<template> for inert, reusable markup) — that let you build reusable, framework-agnostic UI elements. They shine when you need a single widget (a date picker, a video player, a design-system button) that must work identically inside React, Vue, Angular, or plain HTML pages, or when you're shipping a component to third parties who don't share your build tooling. They're a poor fit for building an entire application: you lose a framework's ergonomics around state management, routing, and data binding, and have to hand-roll reactivity yourself.
note: Shadow DOM's CSS is scoped automatically — the page's global stylesheet cannot accidentally restyle <hello-badge>, and its internal styles can't leak out either.

question: How Do You Add SEO Meta Tags and Structured Data (Open Graph & JSON-LD)?
description: Beyond <title> and <meta name="description">, rich search and social results rely on two extra layers. Open Graph tags (og:title, og:description, og:image, og:type) control how a page previews when shared on Facebook, LinkedIn, or Slack — without them, platforms fall back to guessing from page content, often badly. Twitter/X reads its own twitter:card tags, falling back to Open Graph if absent. schema.org structured data, embedded as a JSON-LD <script type="application/ld+json"> block, describes entities (an Article, Product, Recipe, FAQ) in a machine-readable format that search engines use to render rich results — star ratings, breadcrumbs, FAQ accordions — directly in search listings. JSON-LD is preferred over microdata/RDFa because it's a separate block that doesn't clutter your visible markup.
code:
<head>
  <title>10 MongoDB Indexing Tips</title>
  <meta name="description" content="Practical indexing strategies for production MongoDB clusters.">

  <!-- Open Graph -->
  <meta property="og:type" content="article">
  <meta property="og:title" content="10 MongoDB Indexing Tips">
  <meta property="og:description" content="Practical indexing strategies for production MongoDB clusters.">
  <meta property="og:image" content="https://example.com/og-image.png">

  <!-- Structured data -->
  <script type="application/ld+json">
  {
    "@context": "https://schema.org",
    "@type": "Article",
    "headline": "10 MongoDB Indexing Tips",
    "author": { "@type": "Person", "name": "Jane Doe" },
    "datePublished": "2024-01-15"
  }
  </script>
</head>
note: Validate structured data with Google's Rich Results Test — a single missing required field silently disqualifies the page from rich results.

question: What Is the Difference Between Progressive Enhancement and Graceful Degradation?
description: Both aim for a site that works across varying browser capabilities, but they start from opposite ends. Progressive enhancement builds a functional baseline first — solid semantic HTML that works with no CSS and no JavaScript (a form that still submits via a normal POST, content that's readable unstyled) — then layers on CSS for presentation and JavaScript for enhanced interactivity (client-side validation, AJAX submission, animations) for browsers that support it. Graceful degradation works the other way: build the full, rich experience first, then add fallbacks for when something isn't supported. Progressive enhancement is generally considered more robust and accessible, because the baseline never depends on JavaScript loading successfully — it degrades naturally rather than requiring you to anticipate every failure mode.
code:
<!-- Baseline: works with zero JS -->
<form action="/search" method="GET">
  <input type="search" name="q" required>
  <button type="submit">Search</button>
</form>

<script>
  // Enhancement: intercept and use fetch for a smoother experience,
  // but only if JS actually runs.
  document.querySelector('form').addEventListener('submit', async (e) => {
    if (!window.fetch) return; // let the native GET submission happen
    e.preventDefault();
    const q = new FormData(e.target).get('q');
    const results = await fetch(`/api/search?q=${encodeURIComponent(q)}`);
    // render results in place, no full page reload
  });
</script>
note: If the <script> tag fails to load entirely, the form above still works — that's the defining test of progressive enhancement.

question: How Do <picture> and srcset Implement Responsive, Art-Directed Images?
description: The srcset attribute on lets the browser choose the best image from a list of candidates based on device pixel density or viewport width, paired with a sizes attribute that tells it how much space the image will occupy at each breakpoint — this solves the 'serve the right resolution' problem without JavaScript. goes further, enabling true art direction (swap to an entirely different crop on mobile, not just a smaller version) and format fallback (offer modern formats like AVIF or WebP first, falling back to JPEG for browsers that don't support them) via multiple elements, each with its own media or type condition, with a plain as the required fallback.
note: The browser evaluates <source> elements top-to-bottom and picks the first matching, supported one — order format alternatives from most to least modern.

question: What HTML5 Form Validation Attributes and the Constraint Validation API Should You Know?
description: HTML5 ships built-in client-side validation via attributes: required, pattern (a regex the value must match), min/max and step for numeric or date inputs, minlength/maxlength, and typed inputs like email or url that validate format automatically. The browser blocks submission and shows a native tooltip when these fail, and the :valid/:invalid CSS pseudo-classes let you style fields accordingly. For custom logic beyond what attributes express, the Constraint Validation API gives you programmatic control: element.checkValidity() runs validation and returns a boolean, element.validity exposes which specific constraint failed (valueMissing, patternMismatch, tooShort, etc.), and element.setCustomValidity('message') lets you inject a custom error — including cross-field checks like 'passwords must match' — that plugs into the same native reporting UI via reportValidity().
code:
<form id="signup">
  <input type="password" id="pw" required minlength="8">
  <input type="password" id="pw2" required>
  <button type="submit">Create Account</button>
</form>

<script>
  const pw2 = document.getElementById('pw2');
  document.getElementById('signup').addEventListener('submit', (e) => {
    const pw = document.getElementById('pw').value;
    if (pw2.value !== pw) {
      pw2.setCustomValidity('Passwords must match');
    } else {
      pw2.setCustomValidity('');
    }
    if (!e.target.checkValidity()) e.preventDefault();
  });
</script>
note: setCustomValidity must be reset to an empty string once the field becomes valid again, or the browser will keep treating it as permanently invalid.
